[0] everyday_reading (E): In everyday reading of `INPUT A` or `readInt`, the command looks like it inputs the letter A, or 'looks at' a number without using it up. In fact a read takes the next token from the input stream, converts it, and returns the value, which the program must store (e.g. int a = StdIn.readInt()).
[1] misconception (M) -> StdInRereads: wrong rule: Calling StdIn.readInt() twice returns the same value twice. Right rule: Each read consumes its value, so the second call returns the next value.
[2] misconception (M) -> RereadIntoVariableInvalid: wrong rule: Reading a second input value into a variable that already holds one is an error, so the program cannot run. Right rule: A later read assigns a new value, which overwrites the old one. y = StdIn.readInt(); y = StdIn.readInt(); is legal, and y keeps the second value.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> StdInRereads: Points to LT (each call blocks, then consumes exactly one token, in order). An uneven trace gives a variable a value that was already consumed, skips a token on some reads, or merges two READs into one. (here mixing in: "Calling StdIn.readInt() twice returns the same value twice")
[4] misconception (M) -> NextLineAfterNextInt: wrong rule: A line read after a number read returns the next line typed. Right rule: readInt() stops right after the number and leaves the rest of that line, including the line separator. A following readLine() returns that rest (often ""), not the next line.
[5] misconception (M) -> InputReadOnceBeforeLoop: wrong rule: Reading a value once before the loop is enough; the loop will process each new input value. Right rule: A loop must call a read inside its body on every pass. A single read before the loop gives one value, which is processed over and over.

[0] names_the_element (N): StdIn is a booksite library of static methods that read typed values from the standard input stream: isEmpty, readInt, readDouble, readLong, readBoolean, readChar, readString, readLine, readAll.
[1] states_the_rule (S): StdIn reads from a stream that may be empty or may contain values separated by whitespace. readInt() reads the next token, parses it as an int and returns it, and the token must have the type the method expects. Outside the book's StdIn library, standard Java reads keyboard input with java.util.Scanner (nextInt(), nextDouble(), nextLine()); a token of the wrong type stops the program with InputMismatchException.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): When execution reaches a read, the program blocks until a complete token is available (at the terminal, until <return>). The read then parses the token and returns, the assignment stores the value, and the next statement runs.
[1] output_prediction (OP): readInt returns an int, readDouble a double, readString a String, readBoolean a boolean. AddInts 4 with input 144 233 377 1024 prints Sum is 1778.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One read moves the input position past one token and returns its value. Assigning that value overwrites the variable's previous value. No other variable changes.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Every StdIn call takes from the same stream position, so values are delivered once, in order.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): To read an unknown number of values, each read must be guarded by !StdIn.isEmpty() as the condition of a while loop whose body reads.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): With `< file` the same StdIn calls read from the file instead of the keyboard. The program text does not change.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): The reads must follow the file's layout: one readInt() for n first, then pairs of readInt() for each link i j until isEmpty().
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): The program turns the input stream into the output stream: values read with StdIn are processed and the results are written with StdOut. The two streams are independent.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): StdIn values can drive StdDraw output. PlotFilter reads x, y pairs and draws a point for each, after scaling from the first four numbers.
[6] relation_to_neighbour (R): The method called fixes the type the next token must have: readInt needs an int literal, and readDouble accepts 5 or 5.0.
[7] relation_to_neighbour (R): Because a read can run at any point in execution, a read inside a loop lets each typed value decide the next branch.
[8] relation_to_neighbour (R): Token reads (readInt, readString) and line reads (readLine) share one position. A token read leaves the rest of its line for the next readLine, so it is best not to mix the two.
[9] relation_to_neighbour (R): Command-line arguments are a fixed number of strings given once when the program starts (args[]); standard input is a stream of any length read while the program runs (StdIn.readInt()). Both arrive as text and must be parsed into numbers.
[10] purpose_of_the_whole (P): StdIn brings an unbounded amount of data into a running program. The variable that receives each read plays the Sajaniemi role of most-recent holder.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> StdInRereads: Changing the input data changes the results without recompiling. Swapping two reads swaps the values the two variables get. Changing readInt to readDouble accepts more inputs; the reverse breaks on tokens like 12.2.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: StdIn/StdOut/StdDraw/StdAudio are not part of Java; their files must be in the working directory or on the classpath. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: StdIn.class is absent when the program runs: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: StdIn. If StdIn.java is absent when compiling, javac reports 'cannot find symbol' instead.
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use StdIn when the amount of data is large or unknown, comes from a file or another program, or must be supplied while the program runs. Use command-line arguments for a few parameters fixed at launch.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The next token must parse as the requested type. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: The next token is not an int literal, e.g. abc, 12.2 or true for readInt(). StdIn throws NumberFormatException in the book's version and InputMismatchException in the booksite/Scanner version.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A read requires a remaining value; test StdIn.isEmpty() first. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: More reads than values: a fixed-count loop with too few inputs, or an unguarded read after EOF.

Command-line arguments are a fixed number of strings given once when the program starts (args[]); standard input is a stream of any length read while the program runs (StdIn.readInt()). Both arrive as text and must be parsed into numbers.
Like StdIn, StdDraw is a library downloaded from the booksite; StdIn brings values into the program, while StdDraw produces drawings as output.
StdIn takes values in from the input stream; StdOut sends values out to the output stream.
A filter reads its data from standard input and writes what it keeps to standard output.
Input format rules apply to every StdIn read.
The graph is read from standard input: first the number of pages n, then the link pairs i j.
Standard input can be read at any time while the program runs, so the user can type values that change its control flow during execution.
The read loop repeats StdIn reads until StdIn.isEmpty() returns true.
< file makes the contents of the file the standard input stream.
They are standard-input operations.
StdIn reads a stream: values arrive in order and each value is consumed once.
